title: Ang 578–584: the Alahnian
tomorrow: what happened when the herons tried to swim like the swans?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ghorian: the body as the horse the Lord made, carrying the soul to the Beloved's door. Ride home. Same raga today, a very different song.

The sympathy-card aisle runs on a short list of soft words: sorry, loss, thinking of you. Guru Nanak's songs for the dead, the Alahnian, open on ang 578 with a word you won't find on any of those cards. Blessed. Blessed is the Creator, the true King, who set the whole world to its work. That's today's puzzle. Why would a dirge begin with praise?
screen: `SORRY. LOSS. THINKING OF YOU.` → `A DIRGE THAT OPENS: BLESSED.` → `WHY PRAISE AT A FUNERAL?`

segments.voice: Start with the form. Alahnian were laments, the mourning songs of Punjab, and Guru Nanak sets his in Vadhans, a few pages after the wedding-horse songs. Same raga, the horse and the grave. Now the hymns, in paraphrase. Whoever has come must rise and go; this world is a passing show. Then, on ang 579, the line people quote: don't call death bad, people, if you know how to truly die. Dying well, in these songs, means having lived toward the True One, serving and remembering, so the road ahead is open. And there's the answer to the puzzle. The praise comes first because it sets the death inside something bigger: the same Creator who started the world and its work is the one the soul returns to. The opening word doesn't cancel the grief. These are still songs for the dead, sung where people mourn. What it does is give the grief a floor to stand on. A gentle note for parents: today's lesson is about death, so a younger listener might want you nearby. Worth knowing: in the Granth, the raga that holds the wedding songs holds the funeral songs too, a few pages apart.
screen: `A MOURNING FORM, IN VADHANS.` · `WHOEVER HAS COME MUST GO.` · `DON'T CALL DEATH BAD, IF YOU KNOW HOW.` · `PRAISE GIVES GRIEF A FLOOR.` · then, large: `THE DIRGES.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and paper and write the name of someone you miss, or someone grieving right now. Under it, write one true thing about how that person lived or loves. Rest your hand on the page for the rest of the sit and let the name be there with you.
Ang 578. Where Guru Nanak's Alahnian begin: songs for the dead that open by calling the Creator blessed.
For the road: the dirges, where grief is sung and praise holds it up. Ang 578, read.

howItsDone: At Sikh funerals and in the days after, families gather for kirtan and a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; Guru Nanak's Alahnian in Vadhans are among the hymns that speak to death.
